headline: Rhode Island schools will need cardiac emergency plans and AED access
dek: A law signed in June and highlighted at a State House ceremony this week expands defibrillator requirements and sets a 2027-28 deadline for response plans at public and private middle and high schools.
body: Rhode Island officials are putting a statewide cardiac-emergency standard in place for middle and high schools. Gov. Dan McKee joined lawmakers at the State House on Oct. 15 for a ceremonial signing of legislation that expands automated external defibrillator requirements and requires schools to prepare written plans for sudden cardiac arrests.

The law applies to public and private middle schools and high schools. Under the enacted text, those schools must provide and maintain functional AEDs in quantities and locations deemed adequate by the education commissioner in consultation with the health director. When a school facility is being used for a school-sponsored activity or an athletic contest is held elsewhere, administrators must ensure that at least one person trained in CPR and AED operation is present. The statute allows training by qualified personnel, including municipal fire and police employees. Source: Rhode Island General Assembly, https://www.rilegislature.gov/pressrelease/_layouts/15/ril.pressrelease.inputform/DisplayForm.aspx?ID=376879&List=c8baae31-3c10-431c-8dcd-9dbbe21ce3e9.

The legislation was formally signed into law in June; the October event was a public ceremony marking the measure. The bill text sets the main planning requirements to begin in the 2027-2028 school year. By then, each middle and high school must develop a cardiac emergency response plan, or CERP, covering how school personnel will respond when someone suffers sudden cardiac arrest or a similar life-threatening emergency on school grounds.

The CERP requirements are more specific than simply keeping a defibrillator in a building. The plan must use evidence-based elements, identify appropriate AED placement, keep devices clearly marked and accessible in an unlocked location, and provide for testing and maintenance. Schools must notify the appropriate emergency medical services provider about each AED and its location. The law also calls for training appropriate staff in first aid, CPR and AED use, with the CERP determining which personnel are covered; the statute specifically lists licensed coaches, school nurses and athletic trainers among possible trainees. Source: 2026-H 7027, Rhode Island General Assembly, https://webserver.rilegislature.gov/BillText26/HouseText26/H7027.pdf.

Athletic programs face a separate planning requirement. Beginning in the same 2027-2028 school year, each middle or high school with an athletic department or organized program must create a venue-specific athletic emergency action plan. It must address sudden cardiac arrest and similar emergencies during practices or events, be posted and distributed, and be rehearsed annually. An AED must be clearly marked and accessible at each athletic venue during a school-sponsored practice or event, and high school and middle-school coaches must maintain first-aid, CPR and AED training.

That schedule gives districts time to determine where devices belong, coordinate with local emergency medical services and train staff, but it also means the law does not create an overnight change in every school’s readiness. The education commissioner, working with the health department director, may adopt implementation rules and must establish a process to monitor compliance. Local education agencies may accept gifts, grants and donated equipment to help pay for AED purchases, maintenance and training.

Rhode Island already asks school districts to work with police, fire departments and state emergency officials on broader school safety plans. The Rhode Island Department of Education says school committees must update those plans and procedures annually and describes emergency preparation as a shared responsibility among administrators, educators, first responders and state agencies: https://ride.ri.gov/students-families/health-safety/emergency-preparedness. The new cardiac provisions add a focused medical-response layer to that existing planning structure.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention separately identifies rapid action as the reason for a CERP. In guidance updated Sept. 9, the agency says roughly 23,000 sudden cardiac arrests occur in children each year and emphasizes trained response teams, accessible AEDs, coordination with EMS, communication and practice drills. The CDC also says bystander CPR can double or triple the odds of surviving an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: https://www.cdc.gov/heart-disease/php/cardiac-arrest-response-plans/index.html.

For Rhode Island families, the next meaningful milestones are the state’s implementation guidance and each school’s plan for staffing, device placement and athletic venues. The law establishes the deadline and core safeguards; schools and state education and health officials still have to translate those requirements into plans that can be found, practiced and used before an emergency occurs.
location: Rhode Island public and private middle and high schools
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: Rhode Island schools to add cardiac response plans and AED access
seoDescription: Rhode Island’s new school-safety law expands AED requirements and requires cardiac emergency and athletic response plans at public and private middle and high schools beginning in 2027-28.
